title: Career Roadmap: Tech Policy Analyst
summary: A Tech Policy Analyst studies how technologies affect society and how laws, regulations, government policies, and industry practices should respond to technological developments.

facts.Current degree: Liberal Arts / Liberal Studies – Data, Society & Technology

about.label: Suitable For
about.text: Students interested in technology, public policy, data governance, digital rights, regulation, and the societal impact of emerging technologies

about.label: Primary Work Settings
about.text: Technology companies, public policy think tanks, government advisory organisations, research institutions, consulting firms, NGOs, and digital rights organisations

blocks.text: A Tech Policy Analyst studies how technologies affect society and how laws, regulations, government policies, and industry practices should respond to technological developments.

The role combines technology literacy, policy research, legal and regulatory awareness, social science, economics, and analytical writing. Tech Policy Analysts help organisations understand regulatory changes, assess social and economic implications, and develop evidence-based recommendations.

Unlike a purely technical software role, this career focuses on the relationship between technology, people, institutions, and public policy. Technical knowledge is valuable, but the ability to interpret policy and communicate its implications is equally important.
Typical responsibilities

items.text: Monitor technology-related laws, regulations, government consultations, and policy announcements.
Research the implications of artificial intelligence, data protection, cybersecurity, digital platforms, and emerging technologies.
Analyse how technology policies affect citizens, businesses, governments, and vulnerable communities.
Prepare policy briefs, regulatory summaries, research reports, and executive presentations.
Evaluate technology governance proposals and identify potential benefits, risks, and implementation challenges.
Compare technology policy approaches across countries and jurisdictions.
Coordinate with legal teams, engineers, researchers, economists, and public affairs professionals.
Support stakeholder consultations and discussions with policymakers, industry bodies, and civil society.
Analyse public datasets and research findings to support recommendations.
Track policy developments and communicate relevant changes to decision-makers.

blocks.label: Example
blocks.text: If a government proposes new rules for AI-generated content, a Tech Policy Analyst may assess the proposal's implications for innovation, privacy, misinformation, competition, and individual rights.
The recommended programme is Liberal Arts or Liberal Studies with a concentration in Data, Society & Technology.
This interdisciplinary pathway is particularly relevant because technology policy requires an understanding of both technical systems and their social consequences.

blocks.text: C. Complementary technical preparation
Students do not need to become full-time software engineers, but they should understand how data systems, algorithms, AI models, and digital platforms operate.
Recommended foundations include Python, SQL, spreadsheets, statistics, and the ability to interpret technical documentation.
AI Governance and Policy
Studies AI regulation, model accountability, transparency, safety, bias, responsible deployment, and the effects of AI on society.
Data Protection and Privacy
Analyses personal data collection, consent, data governance, privacy risks, and organisational compliance with applicable laws.
Internet and Digital Platform Governance
Examines content moderation, online safety, platform accountability, misinformation, and the governance of digital services.
Cybersecurity Policy
Focuses on cyber governance, incident reporting requirements, critical infrastructure protection, digital resilience, and national cybersecurity strategy.
Technology Competition and Digital Markets
Studies competition policy, digital monopolies, interoperability, platform economics, and the effects of regulation on innovation.
Digital Inclusion and Technology Equity
Evaluates digital access, accessibility, algorithmic discrimination, digital literacy, and the distribution of technology's benefits and risks.

blocks.text: Essential policy-writing formats
Students should practise producing:

items.text: A one-page technology policy brief.
A regulatory change summary.
An AI system impact assessment.
A comparative policy analysis.
A stakeholder mapping report.
A public consultation submission.
A technology governance risk register.
An executive presentation explaining a proposed policy change.

rows.text: Basic data analysis, text processing, and research automation
Regulatory trackers, comparison tables, and stakeholder databases
Documenting reproducible research and data analysis
Maintaining code, research notebooks, and public project documentation
Discovering academic research and scholarly literature

blocks.text: Use official government and regulator publications as primary sources wherever possible. Secondary commentary can provide context, but it should not replace verification of the original document.
A strong portfolio should demonstrate that the student can understand a technology issue, analyse policy implications, and present practical recommendations.
Project 1
AI Governance Policy Brief
Analyse a current AI governance issue, such as transparency, algorithmic bias, AI-generated misinformation, or accountability.
Deliverables:

items.text: A two-page policy brief
Problem definition and current policy context
Stakeholder interests and possible impacts
Three evidence-based recommendations
Official sources and research references

blocks.text: Project 2
India Technology Regulation Tracker
Create a spreadsheet tracking selected technology-related laws, draft rules, consultations, notifications, responsible authorities, and implementation dates.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: A structured tracker, source links, document status, update dates, and a concise monthly policy summary.
Project 3
AI Impact Assessment
Select a hypothetical AI system used in recruitment, education, healthcare administration, or customer service.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: A description of the system, affected stakeholders, possible bias and privacy risks, accountability questions, risk mitigation measures, and limitations of the assessment.
Project 4
Comparative International Technology Policy
Compare how two or three jurisdictions approach a topic such as AI governance, data protection, or online safety.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: A comparison matrix, differences in regulatory approaches, implementation challenges, and lessons that may be relevant to India. Distinguish legal requirements from voluntary frameworks.
Project 5
Digital Inclusion Data Analysis
Use a reliable public dataset to examine digital access, internet adoption, accessibility, or technology usage across selected populations or regions.

blocks.label: Deliverables
blocks.text: A reproducible analysis, charts, a methodology note, limitations, and policy recommendations grounded in the data.

blocks.label: Title
blocks.text: Governing Artificial Intelligence in India: Innovation, Accountability, and Public Interest

blocks.label: Objective
blocks.text: Examine how AI governance approaches can balance innovation, economic opportunity, public safety, privacy, fairness, and accountability.
Project methodology

items.text: Define a specific research question related to AI governance.
Collect official Indian policy documents, regulatory materials, and relevant international frameworks.
Review academic research and credible policy publications.
Identify stakeholders, including government bodies, technology developers, businesses, civil society, researchers, and affected communities.
Compare alternative governance approaches and their trade-offs.
Develop an impact matrix covering innovation, rights, safety, implementation cost, and enforceability.
Formulate practical, evidence-based recommendations.
Present the findings in a written report and an executive briefing.

blocks.text: Expected deliverables

items.text: A 15–25-page research report, depending on university requirements.
A two-page policy brief.
A comparative policy matrix.
A stakeholder map.
A regulatory monitoring spreadsheet.
A final presentation with source references.

blocks.label: Evaluation criteria
blocks.text: Technical understanding, source reliability, quality of analysis, balanced reasoning, policy relevance, and clarity of communication.

The project should clearly distinguish between enacted law, draft proposals, government strategies, voluntary standards, and the student's own recommendations. Verify the status of all regulatory documents as of the submission date.

blocks.text: Admission requirements differ by programme. Law degrees, in particular, have specific eligibility conditions, and an LLM generally requires a qualifying law degree.

A postgraduate degree is not always required for junior policy research roles. It becomes more useful when the desired position demands deeper technical, quantitative, legal, or specialised policy expertise.

Career progression depends on the organisation, demonstrated analytical ability, domain expertise, qualifications, and professional experience.

blocks.label: AI regulation and governance
blocks.text: Organisations need to understand emerging rules, standards, accountability mechanisms, and AI-related risks.

blocks.label: Data protection and privacy
blocks.text: Data-intensive services create ongoing demand for policy analysis and governance expertise.

blocks.label: Digital competition
blocks.text: Platform markets, interoperability, and competition concerns remain important policy topics.

blocks.label: Cybersecurity governance
blocks.text: Critical infrastructure and digital resilience require coordination between technical, policy, and institutional stakeholders.

blocks.label: Cross-border technology regulation
blocks.text: Differences between national approaches create demand for comparative policy analysis.

blocks.label: Algorithmic accountability
blocks.text: Governments and organisations increasingly need methods for evaluating automated decisions and their impacts.

blocks.label: Digital inclusion
blocks.text: Policy work must address accessibility, digital literacy, affordability, and unequal access.

blocks.label: Technology impact assessment
blocks.text: Organisations can benefit from structured evaluation of how technologies affect people, institutions, and markets.

blocks.label: AI-assisted policy research
blocks.text: AI can support document review and summarisation, but source verification, judgement, and accountability remain essential.

blocks.label: Evidence-driven policymaking
blocks.text: The ability to combine technical understanding, quantitative analysis, and clear writing can differentiate candidates.

The strongest candidates will combine technology literacy, policy reasoning, research quality, and communication skills rather than relying on only technical knowledge or only theoretical policy knowledge.
Use this checklist to assess preparation for Tech Policy Analyst roles.
Readiness self-assessment
0 of 12
Understand the relationship between technology, society, regulation, and public policy.
Explain core concepts in AI, data systems, digital platforms, and cybersecurity.
Find and verify technology policy information from official sources.
Write a concise policy brief on a current technology governance issue.
Compare regulatory approaches across at least two jurisdictions.
Use spreadsheets and basic data analysis to support a policy argument.
Build a technology regulation tracker with dates, sources, and document status.
Create a stakeholder map for a technology policy issue.
Complete an AI impact assessment or comparable governance project.
Understand the difference between enacted law, draft proposals, and voluntary standards.
Complete a relevant internship, supervised research project, or policy simulation.
Build a portfolio with at least three high-quality policy or analytical work samples.
Mark an item complete once you can demonstrate the skill through a project, report, or relevant experience.
By graduation, a student pursuing a Tech Policy Analyst career should aim to demonstrate:

items.text: A multidisciplinary understanding of technology, data, society, economics, and public policy.
Familiarity with AI governance, data protection, digital rights, and technology regulation.
The ability to find, interpret, and verify official policy documents.
Strong analytical writing, critical thinking, and presentation skills.
Basic competence in Python, SQL, spreadsheets, or other appropriate analytical tools.
The ability to assess policy trade-offs and explain technology's potential societal impacts.
Practical experience through internships, research projects, or policy simulations.
A portfolio containing policy briefs, comparative analyses, stakeholder maps, and regulatory trackers.
Professional judgement, research integrity, and awareness of privacy and ethical responsibilities.

blocks.label: Recommended first milestone
blocks.text: Choose one technology policy topic—such as AI governance, data privacy, or digital inclusion—and prepare a two-page policy brief supported by official sources. Build a regulatory tracker alongside it, then use both as the foundation of a portfolio for Tech Policy Analyst internships and entry-level roles.
